title: The table matters
hookLine: the biggest portion may suit your stomach, but not the fellowship of the table (Enchiridion 36)
carry: for the sake of the fellowship

lines: FOUR PIECES LEFT. ONE IS BIGGEST.
cards: A platter comes around the table. Four pieces of chicken left, and one of them is clearly the biggest. Everyone sees it.
Everyone pretends not to. There's a small, silent negotiation going on, and you may have been on both sides of it. Epictetus, of all people, uses this moment to teach a bit of logic.
Section thirty-six of the Enchiridion starts like a textbook on reasoning and ends at a dinner party.

teach.h: DAY OR NIGHT: TRUE. DAY AND NIGHT: FALSE.
teach.b: Take two statements: it is day, it is night. Joined with or, it is day or it is night, they make a perfectly good statement. Joined with and, it is day and it is night, they make a false one.
Same pieces, different combination. The value depends on how they're joined.

teach.h: THE BIGGEST PORTION, JOINED TO THE TABLE.
teach.b: In the same way, Epictetus says, at a shared meal, taking the biggest portion may have value for your body taken alone. But joined to the table, to the company and the host, it loses that value.
So the larger share is to be avoided, for the sake of the fellowship of the meal. When you eat with someone, he says, don't only weigh what the food on your plate is worth to your body.
Keep in view the respect owed to your host. The meal isn't just food. It's a relationship being kept, one plate at a time.
Back in section fifteen, life was a banquet, and the lesson was to take a modest share when the dish reaches you.

teach.h: THE SMALLER PORTION HONORS THE TABLE.
teach.b: Today goes one step further: the smaller portion isn't only self-control, it's a way of honoring the people at the table. And a look back at the week, since today closes it: mostly quiet. Yes means yes.
He missed the rest. Wait. No need to hide.
Every one of them, like today's, is about living well alongside other people.

how: Some people practicing Stoicism take the smaller share at shared meals and let others choose first, as a small way of honoring the company and the host.

o: a private feast eaten alone, away from the crowd
life pictured as a shared meal where you take your share
a contest to see who can eat the most at one sitting

games.q: the table matters — tap the pairs.
p: it is day or it is night
it is day and it is night

s: Epictetus says the bigger portion has no value at all
it may have value for the body; joined to the shared table, it loses it.
section thirty-six begins with a point of logic
day or night is true; day and night is false. the joining changes the value.

games.q: the platter reaches you. four pieces left, one clearly biggest. what does Epictetus suggest?
o: take the biggest. it's good for your body.
leave the biggest, for the sake of the table and the host.
take two, so nobody has to choose.
games.why: the big portion may suit the body, he says, but keep the fellowship of the meal and the respect owed the host in view.

practice: Picture the next meal you'll share, at home, at work, anywhere: the table, the faces, the food going around. See yourself quietly taking the smaller portion, or letting someone else choose first, with no announcement.
Notice how it feels to put the table ahead of your plate for a moment, then let the picture go and just breathe.

wordCard.voice: Banquet. Life as a shared meal, Epictetus says elsewhere; the biggest portion may suit your body, but not the fellowship of the table. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a drinking party or banquet, where English symposium comes from; Epictetus' shared meal.

carryVoice: Your line: for the sake of the fellowship. The host and the company count too. Day three hundred seventy-one, and the week is done.
